title: Harrow Glen Rising
premise: Paloma Nakamura, a pest controller in the decaying town of Harrow Glen, has spent five years ignoring the sounds inside the old Aldous house—until a client's sleep-recording device captures something answering questions in her own dead mother's voice. Digging into county archives, Paloma learns that in 1974 the town's founding families buried a child beneath the house to seal a bargain that keeps Harrow Glen prosperous, and that the thing below has been collecting voices ever since. As neighbors who once ignored her begin to remember her name—and want her gone—Paloma must choose between the belonging she's always craved and returning what was taken, even if it means giving back the only recording of her mother's voice. In the end she unearths the child's remains and burns the covenant ledger, freeing the trapped voices but leaving Harrow Glen to collapse into honest ruin; Paloma walks out of town alone for the first time, finally audible to herself.
about_author: A. M. Reyes is the pen name of a former building inspector from rural Ohio who spent a decade documenting houses no one wanted to enter. Their fiction draws on small-town decay, family silence, and the conviction that every old house keeps minutes of its meetings.

chapters.title: The Client on Corliss Street
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. A routine bedbug call at the Aldous house introduces Paloma to Marisol Vane and her daughter's complaints of 'the answering man.' Paloma finds no pests but notices fine scratches behind the baseboards, arranged like writing. The beat is professional detachment beginning to crack.

chapters.title: Five Years of Explanations
chapters.summary: POV Paloma, with flashbacks. We learn why Paloma came to Harrow Glen: after her mother's death, invisibility felt like safety. She catalogs past noises in the town with rational causes. The emotional beat is the comfort—and cost—of deliberate blindness.

chapters.title: What the Recorder Caught
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. Reviewing her daughter's sleep recordings, Marisol hears a second voice answering questions no one asked aloud. She plays it for Paloma, who recognizes the cadence before the words: it speaks in her mother's rhythms. Beat: dread arriving through intimacy.

chapters.title: Scratches Behind the Walls
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. Investigating the walls, Paloma finds layers of names scratched into the plaster, dated across decades, each crossed out. Her own childhood nickname is among them, uncrossed. Beat: the horror of being already known by something she never met.

chapters.title: The Founding Families
chapters.summary: POV Paloma at the county archive. She discovers the 1974 covenant: seven families, one deed clause, a sealed annex never opened. The librarian, an old Vane cousin, goes pale and asks her to leave. Beat: the first door closing because she asked the right question.

chapters.title: Everyone Remembers My Name
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. Overnight, townspeople who ignored her for years greet her warmly, offer favors, invite her to supper. The attention feels like sunlight and like bait. Beat: belonging offered too easily, and the suspicion that kindness here is currency.

chapters.title: Dinner with the Deacons
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. At a lavish dinner, patriarch Ellery Deacon probes what she found in the archive, then warns her gently about 'towns that keep their promises.' He returns her mother's locket, lost since childhood. Beat: power showing its soft face, corruption wearing hospitality.

chapters.title: The Second Voice Answers Me
chapters.summary: POV Paloma, alone at night. Paloma sets up her own recorder and asks questions. The voice answers—her mother's voice—describing 1974 in fragments: a child, a cellar, seven signatures. Beat: grief weaponized; love used as a hook.

chapters.title: Marisol's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. Desperate to protect her daughter, Marisol secretly offers the house's presence her own voice in exchange for the girl's. Paloma catches her mid-ritual. Beat: love against duty, mirrored—two women willing to pay with themselves.

chapters.title: The Annex Is Opened
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. Forced or permitted—the text blurs which—the sealed annex stands open. Inside: the covenant ledger, photographs of a child named Ivo Aldous, and a wall of labeled jars, each holding a strip of recorded tape. Beat: the machinery of the bargain made physical.

chapters.title: Ivo, 1974
chapters.summary: POV interlude, Ivo Aldous. A short chapter in the buried child's voice: how his family traded him for prosperity, how he learned to speak through walls, how he began collecting voices so he wouldn't be alone. Beat: horror recontextualized as loneliness.

chapters.title: Return What Was Taken
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. The voice states its terms plainly: return Ivo to the light, burn the ledger, and everyone goes free—or refuse, and it keeps collecting, starting with Marisol's daughter. Beat: duty crystallizing into a deadline; time already running out.

chapters.title: The Town Closes Ranks
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. The warmth curdles: her truck is vandalized, her contracts canceled, Deacon's people watch her house. The town needs the bargain intact more than it needs its children safe. Beat: belonging revealed as ownership.

chapters.title: My Mother's Voice, Priced
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. Deacon offers Paloma a private deal: keep the tapes, including her mother's recording, and simply walk away. She listens to the whole tape once, sobbing, then says no. Beat: the theme's sharpest edge—love refusing to be bribed.

chapters.title: Marisol Disappears
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. Marisol vanishes; her car sits empty outside the Aldous house. The daughter, sleepwalking, scratches new names into Paloma's own walls. Beat: guilt, urgency, and the realization the house is now reaching beyond its address.

chapters.title: Digging in the Dark
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. Armed with the ledger's map, Paloma breaks into the cellar and begins excavating beneath the hearth while the walls recite every name she's ever been called. Beat: terror sustained through labor; the body found at chapter's end, small and waiting.

chapters.title: The Seven Signatures
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. Confronting the surviving descendants—including a dying Deacon who confesses his father led the burial—she collects their marks on a revocation. Some sign weeping; one attacks her. Beat: complicity confronted generation by generation.

chapters.title: What the House Wants Back
chapters.summary: POV Paloma, deepest night. The house offers its final trade: Ivo's bones for Paloma's voice, forever, so someone will always answer the child. Paloma nearly accepts—until she hears Marisol alive in the walls, singing to him. Beat: the climax's hinge, chosen love over traded self.

chapters.title: Harrow Glen Rising
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. At dawn Paloma carries Ivo's remains into the light, burns the ledger on the lawn as the town watches, and reads every name from the tapes aloud until the walls go quiet. The ground shudders; foundations crack. Beat: catharsis through witness, not violence.

chapters.title: Aftermath of Voices
chapters.summary: POV Marisol. Marisol is found alive, hoarse but herself. The town must reckon with prosperity draining away as the bargain dies; some thank Paloma, most don't. The daughter sleeps silently for the first time in months. Beat: bittersweet accounting of freedom's cost.

chapters.title: The Last Recording
chapters.summary: POV Paloma. Packing to leave, Paloma plays her mother's tape one final time—not to keep the voice, but to say goodbye to it—then lets the tape run blank in the sun. Beat: grief completed rather than preserved.

chapters.title: Audible
chapters.summary: POV Paloma, epilogue. Driving out of Harrow Glen, Paloma stops at the town line, says her full name aloud to no one, and finds it fits. Behind her the town settles into honest ruin; ahead, nothing is listening, and for the first time that feels like peace. Beat: resolution—belonging rebuilt within, not granted without.
